text: This is Momentum's Waypoint, a working delivery workspace for the Tech Triathlon Hackathon. The implementation follows our Designathon journey: request, plan, load, deliver, synchronize, receive, and resolve. The four roles share one database, so a decision made by one person reaches the next person in the workflow. We begin as the store manager at Fresh Colombo outlet two. My Orders shows the chilled replenishment request, its forty crates, and a clear delivery status. Order details preserve the requested date, receiving restrictions, and separate handover checkpoints. The Create Order screen captures handling, units, weight, volume, and notes. The server enforces the four P M Sri Lanka cutoff and operating dates. The supplied calendar ends in June, so the repeatable review fixture uses June twenty fourth, with a clearly displayed fixed walkthrough clock. This is synthetic competition data, not a live delivery operation.

The dispatcher works in Planning. The selected draft uses refrigerated van vehicle thirty five, serving three Fresh Colombo outlets from Peliyagoda. Planning is manual with validation, which the challenge explicitly permits. The dispatcher can assign or remove orders, change the vehicle, reorder stops, create another run, or record an explicit deferral. The system checks weight and volume separately. It also checks refrigeration, depot ownership, van only access, receiving windows, fuel quota, daily route count, and vehicle turnaround. Selecting an ambient van makes the temperature check fail and disables publication. Restoring the refrigerated van restores a feasible plan. Here the mall garment request has a previous deferral and too much volume for this morning run. Its reason and next action remain visible. The oversized appliance request exceeds every individual vehicle and needs a revised split request. We record a deferral instead of silently dropping demand. Stop arrival estimates use supplied district travel and service allowance data, with a documented monsoon buffer. They are planning estimates, not live traffic or a trained prediction. Publishing rechecks every constraint in a database transaction and locks the allocations for loading.

The loader now sees the published manifest on a phone sized screen. The loading list reverses the delivery sequence, so the last delivery stop is loaded first. Outlet three has fifteen of the required twenty crates. This shortage is visible and the final handoff is blocked. The loader reports the five missing crates, which creates a shared dispatcher issue. Replenishment changes the physical count to twenty. Saving the count and verifying it are separate steps, so a corrected number does not accidentally imply a completed check. Every stop must match its planned quantity and be explicitly verified. Once all three quantities are verified, Confirm Loading Handoff releases the manifest to the assigned driver. The server enforces these gates independently of the interface. A driver cannot start a trip while the loading shortage remains unresolved.

The driver uses My Trip while safely stopped. Start Trip becomes available only after the loader releases the manifest. The next checkpoint shows the outlet, expected arrival, and verified quantity. At the first stop the driver records arrival and captures the actual handover. A delivery records the recipient, quantity, exception reason when needed, signature, and photograph. This demonstration draws a signature and uploads a synthetic evidence image. When evidence cannot be captured, the driver must explicitly explain why. The record saves to device storage before a network upload is attempted. At the next stop we disconnect the browser network for a real offline test. The driver can still record forty crates and the recipient. Saving opens Sync, where the handover is clearly pending rather than presented as a synchronized receipt. Reloading while offline preserves the application shell, cached manifest, and queued handover. Restoring connectivity uploads the immutable record. It remains on the device until the server acknowledges it. The unique client identifier and payload hash make retries safe even if an upload succeeded but its response was lost. We complete the final stop and confirm the depot return after all handovers synchronize.

Back at the store, the synchronized handover becomes available for receipt review. The driver recorded forty crates, but the store independently confirms what actually arrived. We enter thirty nine and explain the difference. This creates a receipt discrepancy for the dispatcher; it does not rewrite the driver's recorded forty. In Issues, the dispatcher sees the report and records a resolution with its next action. The delivered and received quantities remain factual in the audit history after the issue is resolved. This separation prevents a driver handover from being mistaken for confirmed store receipt. Across the workflow, progress, shortages, deferrals, and exceptions are shared records rather than isolated browser simulations.

The architecture keeps the implementation small and inspectable. The browser interface and JSON API use the same origin. The Python web service checks hashed sessions, role permissions, outlet ownership, assigned trips, and every workflow transition. PostgreSQL stores normalized orders, trips, stops, deliveries, receipts, issues, and audit events. The original reference rows retain their supplied identifiers and attributes. A Docker Compose command starts the complete application and database and imports the seeds automatically. The SQL adapter also supports SQLite for a dependency free local run. Mutations use transactions, publication reserves weekly fuel atomically, and draft versions reject stale edits. In the browser, a service worker caches application assets, while Indexed D B holds user scoped snapshots, drafts, and the durable delivery queue. Automated integration tests cover the four role handoff, constraints, permissions, cutoff, conflicts, and idempotency. Browser tests also verify real offline reload and reconnect, with no page errors. The repository includes architecture, data model, deployment instructions, AI disclosure, and the numbered judge walkthrough. AI assisted the implementation, tests, documentation, and this synthetic narration. The team remains responsible for reviewing and submitting the final system. Public deployment and the unlisted YouTube upload are verified separately from this local demonstration.
